analysis.one_liner: Replaces private Medicare drug plans with a government-run benefit with no premium and lower, negotiated drug prices.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in August 2008 with 21 House sponsors, all Democrats, never got a hearing or a vote; it died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have repealed the privatized Medicare Part D drug benefit created in 2003 and replaced it with a Medicare-administered drug benefit for all beneficiaries, with no monthly premium. The government would negotiate drug prices directly with manufacturers, pharmacies could not charge enrollees more than the negotiated price, and drug makers would have to sell to pharmacies at their lowest price anywhere. It would also let Americans legally import prescription drugs from Canada and other countries with equivalent safety standards, and require a reasonable-pricing agreement before federally funded medical research is handed to a company as a patent.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries gain the most: a simplified, no-premium drug benefit run by Medicare itself, coverage that pays the full negotiated price of prescriptions, and protection from the 'doughnut hole' gap in coverage under private Part D plans. The bill's findings cite Part D paying on average 30% more for drugs than Medicaid, premium increases, and Americans paying up to five times more than consumers in other countries [S2] [S3]. Consumers generally would gain from legal drug importation, which the bill's findings estimate could save Americans over $38 billion a year [S2] [S3]. Pharmacies would gain guaranteed access to participate in the program and reasonable dispensing fees [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the 2003 private Part D structure and replaces it with a Medicare-run 'Prescription Medicine Benefit for the Aged and Disabled' open to all Medicare beneficiaries, with no enrollment premium [S2] [S3].

Medicare would negotiate a schedule of prices with drug manufacturers, wholesalers, and pharmacies, and participating pharmacies could not charge an enrollee more than the negotiated price even after benefit limits [S3].

Drug makers selling to the U.S. government would have to make drugs available to pharmacies at the lowest of the lowest federal price, their Medicaid 'best price', or the lowest importation price [S3].

The bill would waive import restrictions to allow commercial and personal importation of prescription drugs from Canada, the EU, Japan, Australia, New Zealand, and Switzerland under registration, inspection, and tracking safeguards [S3].

Federal agencies could not convey patents from federally funded health research to a company unless the company first agreed to reasonable pricing with the Secretary of Health and Human Services [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers bear the main cost: lower negotiated prices, mandatory lowest-price sales, spending-target rebates, and importation competition. Private Part D plan insurers lose their entire line of business when the benefit moves back inside Medicare [S2] [S3]. Taxpayers would fund the government's share of the new benefit through appropriations [S3], with the intended offset coming from lower drug prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drug makers and Part D insurers

drawbacks.text: The government would pay 100% of the negotiated price of covered prescriptions for enrollees, funded by appropriations, so unless price negotiations and rebates delivered the projected savings, the federal cost of drug coverage would rise [S3].

The bill repeals the existing Part D program outright and transitions all beneficiaries in one step, a disruption for the tens of millions enrolled in private drug plans and for Medicare Advantage plans, which would be barred from offering Part D coverage [S3].

The price-control machinery is complex and rigid: a 'sustainable growth rate' spending target with automatic manufacturer rebates, a Drug Review Board exempting 'breakthrough' medicines, and determinations that are not subject to administrative or judicial review, which risks blunting rewards for genuinely new drugs [S3].

The bill sets no dollar limit on an enrollee's share beyond the negotiated price rules and relies on a benefit-limit structure whose out-of-pocket protections depend on future Secretary regulations and annual appropriations rather than a guaranteed benefit formula [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For seniors and disabled beneficiaries the potential gains are large — no premium, no doughnut hole, and prices closer to what Medicaid or foreign consumers pay. The honest cost is fiscal risk: the government takes on the entire drug benefit and its savings depend on price negotiation and rebate mechanisms that drug makers would fight hard in practice, and the one-step repeal of Part D would be disruptive for enrollees and plans. The importation and reasonable-pricing provisions are narrower but carry real safety-oversight and administrative burdens.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on the last summer of the 110th Congress and referred to two committees, Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means, which never acted on it, so it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Dennis Kucinich introduced the bill on August 1, 2008, joined by 20 Democratic cosponsors [S1] [S3] [S4].
The same day, it was referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and to the Committee on Ways and Means, and then to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health [S1] [S5].
No hearing, markup, floor action, or vote is recorded; the bill's action history ends with the committee referrals [S5].
The 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, and bills not acted on die with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers and private Part D plan insurers are better off, because the existing Part D structure — with Medicare barred from directly negotiating prices — stayed in place. Medicare beneficiaries continue to buy drugs through private plans at prices the bill's findings say run about 30% above Medicaid's, without the no-premium benefit or importation access the bill would have provided [S2] [S5].

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers and Part D insurers

for.name: Rep. Dennis Kucinich
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to replace Medicare Part D with a government-run, no-premium drug benefit and wrote its findings documenting Part D's higher prices and coverage gaps

for.name: 20 of 233 House Democrats
for.role: Democratic cosponsors, all from the party's progressive wing
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as original cosponsors at introduction

against.name: House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees
against.role: Committees of referral under Democratic chairs
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further recorded action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — during the final months of the Congress

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers
against.role: Industry facing lower negotiated prices, mandatory best-price sales, spending-target rebates, and importation competition
against.what_they_did: The bill's own findings describe Part D as a multi-billion-dollar windfall for manufacturers and note the industry's prices run far above foreign and VA prices; the industry had long opposed Medicare price negotiation and importation

sides.party_line_note: All 21 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats, drawn from the party's progressive wing; no Republican supported the bill and no vote was ever taken to test broader support [S3] [S4].

industries.note: The bill would force manufacturers to sell drugs to pharmacies at their lowest price anywhere, subject them to automatic rebates if program spending exceeds a growth target, expose them to importation competition, and attach reasonable-pricing conditions to patents from federally funded research. The bill's findings call the current Part D setup a windfall worth over $3.7 billion to manufacturers in its first two years [S2] [S3].

industries.industry: Private Medicare Part D plan insurers
industries.note: Repealing the 2003 Part D structure eliminates the private-plan drug benefit these insurers administer, and Medicare Advantage plans would be barred from providing Part D coverage. Their premiums and plan designs, including the coverage gap, are what the bill replaces [S2] [S3].

Pharmacies would have guaranteed access to participate in the program, reasonable dispensing fees, and possible rural bonus payments, but they could charge no more than the government-negotiated price and would face generic-substitution requirements. Community pharmacies in rural areas stand to gain from access guarantees [S3].

Registered wholesalers and pharmacies could legally import cheaper qualifying drugs, a new business line, but would face registration fees of $10,000, inspection fees capped at 1% of import value, chain-of-custody tracking, and regular FDA inspections [S3].
